newsitem.title: EGYPT: Egyptians sleep uneasy after building disaster.
newsitem.headline: Egyptians sleep uneasy after building disaster.

text.p: A wave of angst swept Egypt this week as the disastrous collapse of an apartment block in Cairo reminded Egyptians that thousands of lives may be in danger from the lax enforcement of building regulations.
The collapse last Sunday had an even greater impact because the building lay in a solidly middle-class neighbourhood, where people might expect building standards to be higher.
The 11-storey block, in which at least 63 people were killed, was also a short walk from the home and the office of President Hosni Mubarak in the northeastern district of Heliopolis.
Old buildings often collapse in poorer parts of the city but they are usually smaller and the casualty tolls are lower.

Reacting to public outrage at the incident, the government has used military law and the state of emergency to push through stiff new penalties without recourse to parliament, which does not start its autumn session until next week.
Publicity about the disaster has led to a spate of reports that other buildings are also on the verge of collapse.

Residents of one block of 44 flats, also in Heliopolis, had to leave their homes on Friday when police learnt that the owners had removed some of the concrete structures in the basement to make way for some air conditioning pipes.
Cairo governor Omar Abdel-Akher visited the building and inspected the modifications in a public show that the authorities are determined to clamp down on offenders.
Police are holding the owners of that building for questioning, along with the owner of the one that collapsed and the engineers responsible for renovations in one of the flats.

In the Cairo district of Giza the local authorities evacuated two adjacent buildings there on Friday, the opposition newspaper al-Ahrar said on Saturday. One building is leaning 10 cms (four inches) and would knock down the other if it collapsed, it said.

In the Mediterranean city of Alexandria one eight-storey building is being demolished, also as a direct result of the sudden campaign, and the local planning committee has recommended that people leave three other buildings as soon as possible, said the government newspaper al-Akhbar.
The governor of the Nile Delta province of Gharbia has decreed that no extra floors may be built on top of any existing buildings -- a major cause of such disasters.
But building experts say panic measures can touch only the tip of the iceberg and many Egyptians will have to sleep with danger for many years to come.

"It has been found that 98 percent of the buildings in Medinet Nasr violate the regulations, and 97 percent of of those in Mohandiseen and Dokki," Omayma Salaheddin, the head of the government's building inspectorate, told al-Akhbar.
The three Cairo districts, concrete jungles built mostly in the 1970s and 1980s, house several million people.

"We have one case of seven buildings where the file now contains 380 pages, decrees that building should stop, decrees that building can resume and decrees that building works be dismantled but none have been carried out," she added.
The reality is that Egypt, with 60 million people crammed into the narrow confines of the Nile Valley, has nowhere to house the people whose houses may be in danger.

Gamal Badawi, editor of the opposition newspaper al-Wafd, asked his readers to imagine what would have happened if the government had ordered the Heliopolis building evacuated and demolished before it collapsed.

"Would they have left the building? Or would they have gone to court, written to papers appealing against the decision and hurried to the best architects to buy documents to prove the building is stronger than the Pyramid of Cheops?" he said.

"Probably the government, as usual, would have yielded to the fait accompli to avoid a headache, because it does not have the money to compensate the residents or the means to carry out compulsory eviction orders," he added.
